title: Why are black holes still such a mystery?
description:
Can we really get swallowed by a black hole? And what would actually happen if we did? Black holes are really mysterious and there is still so much we don’t know about them. So, grab your space helmet because we’re getting into some of the biggest questions scientists are still trying to answer.

We speak to science journalist, Caroline Steel, to clear up some of the mysteries around black holes. How do they distort time? Are wormholes real?

We also hear from astrophysicist and postdoctoral researcher Rowina Nathan - she separates fact from fiction and busts some of the most common black hole myths, answering questions from members of the Cosmic Girls Foundation, a global community helping teenage girls engage with space, science and technology.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討黑洞的奧秘與常見迷思。主持人 Hannah Gelbart 邀請 BBC 科學記者 Caroline Steel 與天體物理學家 Ruwina Nathan 共同解答大眾對黑洞的疑問。節目探討了黑洞由大質量恆星死亡坍縮形成、事件視界、重力波與蟲洞理論，並解釋掉入黑洞時發生的「義大利麵化」（ spaghettification ）現象。此外，專家也回應了 Cosmic Girls Foundation 青少年社群的提問，澄清太陽因質量過小不會變成黑洞、天體可在穩定軌道上繞行黑洞，以及遠方觀察者眼中時間看似凍結的物理原理。科學家目前正透過望遠鏡觀測遠古宇宙，持續探索黑洞的未解之謎。
summaryEn: In this episode of the BBC World Service podcast What in the World, host Hannah Gelbart explores the mysteries of black holes alongside BBC science reporter Caroline Steel and astrophysicist Ruwina Nathan. The episode explains how black holes form from the collapse of massive dying stars, how scientists detect them via orbiting stars and gravitational waves, and what happens during the process of "spaghettification" if someone falls in. Addressing questions from members of the Cosmic Girls Foundation, Nathan debunks common myths—clarifying that our Sun is too small to become a black hole, that objects can safely orbit a black hole outside its innermost stable orbit, and that time only appears to freeze at the event horizon from the perspective of a distant observer. Finally, the guests discuss how astronomers use deep-space telescopes to study light from the early universe to uncover how ancient black holes formed.
